title: The plant-parts atlas
subtitle: Summer 1 • Identify before explaining
objective: Identify roots, stem, leaves and flower from plant structures, while distinguishing hidden from absent.

sow.exactOutcome: Identify the parts of a flowering plant (roots, stem, leaves, flower).
sow.alignment: Chronological continuation of the supplied SOW. This lesson develops or reviews the named outcome; it does not claim an accreditation award.

priorLearning: A diagram represents selected features, not every detail.
success: Locate parts on a different plant shape.
Use “not visible” when a view hides evidence.

vocabulary.meaning: A plant part usually below ground.
The structure that connects and supports above-ground parts.
A usually flat plant part attached to a stem.
A reproductive structure of a flowering plant.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one chosen pupil route; pencil; optional ruler; projector or offline HTML.
Optional identified non-toxic potted plant; no uprooting required.
preparation: Print the shared evidence, one response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the worked answers. Prepare an oral, pointing or adult-scribed route where useful.
safety: Use an adult-selected non-toxic plant if available. Do not taste plant material or touch eyes; wash hands after handling.
Do not uproot, cut or pull apart a live specimen. The supplied diagram gives a complete root view.
practicalAlternative: All core reasoning uses the supplied evidence and can be completed in 40 minutes without a live practical.

misconceptions.claim: Every green part is a leaf.
misconceptions.correction: Stems and some flowers can also be green.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether shape, attachment and position support the name.

misconceptions.claim: No visible flower means it is not a flowering plant.
misconceptions.correction: A flowering plant may not have open flowers at the time of observation.
misconceptions.check: Compare no flower visible today with never flowers.

misconceptions.claim: A pot with no visible roots has no roots.
misconceptions.correction: An opaque pot can hide roots.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the view allows us to observe.

access.supported: Short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed reasons; same core scientific goal.
access.standard: Make a short evidence-based explanation or record using the supplied information.
access.stretch: Apply the core idea to a changed case, evaluate evidence or identify a limit.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer seated observation, quiet paired rehearsal, private feedback and a pass from public sharing. Routes respond to current access needs, not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Make a guide another pupil can use
slides.notes: Explain that today is about accurate identification; the next lesson explores jobs in detail.

slides.title: Notice the structure
body: 2. Name one plant part you know.
3. Can a container hide part of it?
slides.notes: 1 yes. 2 accept any correct part. 3 yes, opaque containers can hide roots. Avoid awarding a guessed hidden detail as an observation.

slides.title: I identify the part, then label it
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I trace A below the soil. I call these roots. I follow B up from them: this is the stem. I find C attached to the stem, then D.” Use the labels and point to leader endpoints.

visual.title: Find the four main parts
visual.description: A schematic flowering plant with roots below the soil, an upright stem, leaves attached to the stem and a flower above. Label leaders stop at the named structures.

elements.text: Simplified flowering plant; shapes and sizes vary.

slides.title: I keep names when shapes change
body: A flower need not be large or bright.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “Colour alone cannot identify the part: the small green structure can be a flower. I combine position and structure.” This is a simplified comparison, not a botanical species key.

visual.title: Identify by structure and position
visual.description: Two simplified flowering plants have different leaf shapes and flower appearances, while both possess roots, stems, leaves and flowers. Colours alone do not define the part.

elements.text: Different shapes can have the same part name.

slides.title: I separate seen from hidden
body: I can see the stem and leaves.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “I report what this view shows. I cannot conclude that a flowering plant will never flower just because it has none today.”

visual.title: Hidden is different from absent
visual.description: A shoot appears above an opaque pot. The pot hides its roots. No flower is visible in this observation, which cannot establish that the plant never flowers.

elements.text:
Roots are hidden
inside the pot.
Observation: no flower is visible today.
This view cannot tell us whether it flowers at another time.

slides.title: Atlas partners: point, name, check
slides.notes: W1: A roots, B stem, C leaves, D flower. Reveal labels one at a time in the interactive route. Paper route uses the lettered plant diagram and observation E.

table.caption: Simplified atlas clues; not all plants look identical

slides.title: The observation editor
slides.notes: W2: no roots visible is supported. The opaque pot hides them, so no roots at all is not justified. Ask pupils to improve the flower claim in the same way.
slides.reveal: Report “roots hidden” and “no flower visible today”.

slides.title: A plant has small green flowers. What follows?
slides.notes: Correct second option. If pupils choose first, revisit the two distinct green structures.

options.text: All its green parts must be leaves.
options.feedback: Stems and some flowers can be green too.

options.text: It can still have roots, stem, leaves and flowers.
options.feedback: Part names do not depend on bright flower colour.

options.text: Its hidden roots do not exist.
options.feedback: A blocked view does not prove absence.

slides.title: Choose your science route
slides.notes: Set ONE route. Assess correct placement or clear verbal location, not drawing skill. Allow a pupil to direct an adult drawing. Keep identification separate from later functional explanations.

slides.title: Make your own evidence record
slides.notes: Assess correct placement or clear verbal location, not drawing skill. Allow a pupil to direct an adult drawing. Keep identification separate from later functional explanations.

slides.title: Check what the evidence can show
body: Point to the clue you used.
slides.notes: Shares independent time. Ask for a reason, not just a correct word. Assess correct placement or clear verbal location, not drawing skill. Allow a pupil to direct an adult drawing. Keep identification separate from later functional explanations.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve the shared account
slides.notes: Listen to a selected pupil revision and visibly adopt a scientifically accurate contribution. Offer private, written or partner feedback.
slides.prompt: Which label or observation became more precise?
slides.reveal: Use part names with location clues; say hidden or not visible when evidence is limited.

slides.title: Keep the useful change
slides.notes: Shares review time. Name how a pupil contribution changed a label, method or conclusion. Do not rank pupils.
slides.reveal: Use part names with location clues; say hidden or not visible when evidence is limited.

slides.title: Three final checks
body: E1. Name the branching part usually below soil.
E2. Name the part that bears leaves.
E3. Does no visible flower prove a plant never flowers?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual evidence. Use the answer key and re-teach the specified misconception if needed.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence • Atlas clues
pupilPages.intro: Identify A–D on this simplified plant. Use location and shape clues.

visual.title: Identify A–D on the plant
visual.description: Simplified flowering plant with letter-only leaders: A points to branching roots below soil, B to upright stem, C to leaves, D to flower. Names are for pupils to supply.

elements.text: Simplified flowering plant; shapes and sizes vary.

blocks.text: E • Observation record: a potted shoot has a visible stem and leaves. Its roots are hidden by the pot; no flower is visible today.

blocks.prompt: W1. Name A, B, C and D. Give one location clue.
W2. Improve “the plant in E has no roots or flowers”.

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Build the label key
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: roots / stem / leaves / flower.

blocks.prompt: S1. A branches below soil. Its name is...
S2. B is the upright connecting part. Its name is...
S3. Name C and D using the shared records.
S4. E lets us say...
choices: Roots are hidden by the pot.

blocks.prompt: S5. Name one part you would label on a plant drawing.

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Make the atlas page
pupilPages.intro: Draw a simple plant. Accuracy of labels matters more than artistic detail.

blocks.prompt: M1. Draw and label roots, stem, leaves and flower.
M2. Give one location clue for identifying a leaf.
M3. Can a green part be something other than a leaf? Give an example.
M4. Write one accurate sentence about what E does not show.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Review an unfamiliar view
pupilPages.intro: A photograph shows a tall green stem with narrow leaves. Its base is outside the frame; it has no open flower.

blocks.prompt: T1. Name the two parts that are visible.
T2. Explain why the photograph cannot establish that roots are absent.
T3. Rewrite “this cannot be a flowering plant” as a careful observation.
T4. Design two useful views for a more complete plant atlas. Explain what each would reveal.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. Name the branching part usually below soil.
E2. Name the part that bears leaves.
E3. Does no visible flower prove a plant never flowers?
R1. Which idea did you improve or defend? What evidence helped?
R2. What useful question would you investigate next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 yes. 2 any correctly named plant part. 3 yes.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 A roots, B stem, C leaves, D flower. Location clue: roots branch below the soil, leaves attach along the stem, or flower has petals in this example. W2 roots are hidden by the pot and no flower is visible today; do not infer absence or never flowering.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Second option correct. Green colour alone is not a part identifier; hidden roots cannot be judged absent.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 roots. S2 stem. S3 leaves and flower respectively. S4 roots hidden. S5 any correctly named part with appropriate position if drawn.

answers.label: M1–M4
answers.answer: M1 roots connected below stem, leaves attached to stem, flower attached above; accept variations. M2 flat structure attached to stem, combined with other visible clues. M3 stem or some flowers. M4 e.g. roots cannot be seen inside the pot; no flower is visible at this time.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 stem and leaves. T2 the base is outside the photograph. T3 no open flower is visible in this photograph. T4 e.g. a wider whole-plant view including base and a permitted root diagram or transparent-container view; a close view of an open flower at another appropriate time. Do not require uprooting.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 roots. E2 stem. E3 no; flowering depends on species, maturity and season, among other conditions.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 7, We do 8, hinge 3, independent 12, review 3, exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the named stage time.
BUILD uses the supplied Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful contexts for older pupils. Supported, standard and stretch are selectable routes within the pathway.

Interactive We do: predict first, test against the controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. Shared W tasks offer the equivalent paper discussion. Animation is a teaching representation, not filmed experimental evidence.
Keep constructed evidence separate from actual class observations. Do not invent measurements or require internet research.
Secure core: identify all four parts on the atlas and distinguish a hidden part from an absent part. If names are secure but observation language is not, re-teach the cropped-pot example.

interactive.title: Build the plant atlas
interactive.intro: Choose a part name or careful observation, then inspect the labelled model. Paper locations A–E provide the same clues.

The flower is D in this example.
